For depth extension experiments (\S\ref{sec:atlas}), we extend one pipeline (Pythia-1.4B, nucleus) to d0--d5.

\paragraph{Generation pipeline.}
Starting from a Wikipedia subset as seed text ($\mathcal{D}_0$), each generation cycle proceeds in three steps: (1)~LoRA finetuning \cite{hu2022lora} on $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$, freezing base model weights and training low-rank update matrices ($<$1\% additional parameters; $r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, lr $2{\times}10^{-4}$, batch size 8, 3 epochs, dropout $0.05$, architecture-specific targets); (2)~sampling 5{,}000 passages from the LoRA-finetuned model (max 512 tokens, BOS-seeded, no prompt conditioning) under the specified decoding strategy; (3)~the generated corpus becomes $\mathcal{D}_k$ for the next cycle.
Each depth is produced by a model explicitly trained on the prior depth's data---not by sampling from the unmodified base model.
There is no per-passage lineage across depths, ensuring cross-validation splits do not introduce information leakage.

\paragraph{Reference model.}
All statistical features (\S\ref{sec:method:features}) are computed using a fixed reference model---GPT-2 base (124M)---that is independent of the three generation models.
The reference model computes per-token perplexity for each passage, providing a consistent measurement frame across model families.
In cross-model leave-one-out evaluation (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), the reference model remains fixed even when GPT-2~XL is held out; the partial architectural overlap this introduces is discussed in Limitations.

\subsection{Statistical Feature Design}
\label{sec:method:features}

We extract a feature vector $\mathbf{f}(x)$ comprising 19 candidate features from the reference-model perplexity distribution over each passage $x$; ablation (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features}) shows the top 5 achieve 97.6\% of full-set performance, and variance inflation analysis reveals VIF${>}$10 for 14--16 features, placing the effective independent dimensionality at ${\approx}$4--5.
The features fall into four categories (Table~\ref{tab:features}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{The 19 statistical features comprising $\mathbf{f}(x)$, grouped by category. All perplexity and surprisal features are computed from the reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M).}
\label{tab:features}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llr@{}}
\toprule
Category & Features & $n$ \\
\midrule
Perplexity & mean, var, skewness, kurtosis, & 9 \\
statistics & p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 & \\
\addlinespace
Surprisal & mean, var, entropy & 3 \\
statistics & & \\
\addlinespace

\end{tabular}

2	As large language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\to$data$\to$model loop arises---yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.
3	We formalize \emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K passages spanning 3 model families, 3 decoding strategies, and 4 generation depths.
4	From each passage we extract a compact statistical fingerprint---19 candidate features dominated by perplexity tail statistics, with the top 5 achieving 97.6\% of full-set performance---computed against a fixed reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M).
5	A Random Forest classifier achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy (chance = 25\%; 58.8--82.6\% when excluding the near-perfectly separable d0 class; a zero-shot LLM baseline reaches only 36.2\%), with 90th-percentile perplexity and surprisal variance emerging as consistent depth markers across the studied $3 \times 3$ grid (top-2 importance in 9/9 and 8/9 cells, respectively).
6	Our \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas} reveals that decoding strategy reshapes degradation trajectories rather than merely attenuating them, and we define the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric, finding $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ for extended recursion chains.
7	Cross-model transfer reaches 66.4\% and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\%; temperature sampling induces a d1/d2 AUC inversion that we decompose into a correctable scale component and a residual structural component.
8	Applied to WikiText-103 (546 passages), all three model-specific classifiers achieve $\geq$98.5\% d0 accuracy despite $+$621\% domain shift in mean perplexity; on C4 web-crawl text, false positive rates range from 4.7\% to 22.4\%, concentrated in template content.
9	\end{abstract}

file.content:
\begin{abstract}
As large language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\to$data$\to$model loop arises---yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.
We formalize \emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K passages spanning 3 model families, 3 decoding strategies, and 4 generation depths.
From each passage we extract a compact statistical fingerprint---19 candidate features dominated by perplexity tail statistics, with the top 5 achieving 97.6\% of full-set performance---computed against a fixed reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M).
A Random Forest classifier achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy (chance = 25\%; 58.8--82.6\% when excluding the near-perfectly separable d0 class; a zero-shot LLM baseline reaches only 36.2\%), with 90th-percentile perplexity and surprisal variance emerging as consistent depth markers across the studied $3 \times 3$ grid (top-2 importance in 9/9 and 8/9 cells, respectively).
Our \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas} reveals that decoding strategy reshapes degradation trajectories rather than merely attenuating them, and we define the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric, finding $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ for extended recursion chains.
Cross-model transfer reaches 66.4\% and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\%; temperature sampling induces a d1/d2 AUC inversion that we decompose into a correctable scale component and a residual structural component.
Applied to WikiText-103 (546 passages), all three model-specific classifiers achieve $\geq$98.5\% d0 accuracy despite $+$621\% domain shift in mean perplexity; on C4 web-crawl text, false positive rates range from 4.7\% to 22.4\%, concentrated in template content.
\end{abstract}

file.content:
Our EDD definition (Eq.~\ref{eq:edd}) requires all pairwise AUCs up to depth $d^*$ to exceed $T$, which is well-behaved when AUC decays monotonically---as observed in all our configurations.
However, \citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} show that early recursion can temporarily \emph{improve} model quality, which could produce non-monotonic AUC profiles (e.g., a dip at d1/d2 followed by recovery at d2/d3).
Our cross-strategy transfer results provide an empirical example: training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1-vs-d2 AUC as low as 0.129 (GPT-2~XL) and 0.253 (OLMo), violating the monotonicity assumption.
In such cases EDD would conservatively report a lower value than the deepest discriminable pair, potentially underestimating the true discriminable range; extending EDD to handle non-contiguous discriminable regions is future work.
The choice of threshold $T$ is also application-dependent: at $T{=}0.80$, several cells lose one depth level relative to $T{=}0.75$.

\paragraph{Reference model dependency.}
Surprisal-based features are computed relative to GPT-2 base (124M), introducing partial overlap when GPT-2~XL is held out, though GPT-2~XL holdout accuracy (67.6\%) does not exceed the unrelated OLMo (69.2\%).
The choice of reference model affects feature values; a different reference model may shift absolute feature magnitudes and potentially alter discriminability at depth boundaries.

\paragraph{Additional caveats.}
Detection features degrade under domain shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}; our depth features are likely susceptible.
\citet{falahati2026_curated} show that curated synthetic data need not trigger collapse, attenuating the fingerprints we exploit.

\section*{Ethics Statement}
